content:
Some who left Islam say that what turned them away was a single account: a woman of Khaybar whose father and husband were killed, who was taken captive and then married to the Prophet ﷺ the same day. They put it as rape, and they ask how such a man could be a prophet. The account concerns a real woman, Ṣafiyya bint Ḥuyayy, and it touches the hardest questions in the sources about war, captivity and consent.

These six entries set out what the sound reports say and do not say, what the Quran lays down for captive women, and which parts remain hard. The article names no living person. It concedes that she was a captive, that her relatives were killed in war, and that classical law did not make a slave woman's consent a condition of her master's rights. It does not concede what the sources do not say. The related articles are slavery in Islam, the Prophet's marriages and the Jewish tribes of Medina.

In al-Bukhari, Anas reports that when the Prophet ﷺ conquered Khaybar, the captives were collected, and Diḥya asked for a slave girl from among them. The Prophet ﷺ told him to take one, and he took Ṣafiyya bint Ḥuyayy. A man came and said that she was "the chief mistress of the tribes of Quraidha and An-Nadir and she befits none but you". The Prophet ﷺ asked for her to be brought, told Diḥya to take another girl, "then manumitted her and married her".[1]

Thābit asked Anas what the Prophet ﷺ gave as her dowry, and Anas said, "Her self was her Mahr for he manumitted her and then married her."[2] Another report says that her husband "had been killed while she was a bride", that the Prophet ﷺ selected her, and that he set out with her until Sadd al-Rawḥāʾ, "where her menses were over and he married her".[3]

The reports are consistent. She was a captive, she was freed, and the marriage followed the freeing. Verdict: this is what the sound reports say. They are the baseline for the questions below.

The reports say nothing of force on the day of capture or on the night of the battle. They say the opposite on timing. The Prophet ﷺ waited until her menstrual period was over, which is how the waiting rule for captive women was kept, and he consummated the marriage on the road between Khaybar and Medina after he had stayed three days.[4] The claim that he took her "the same day" he killed her husband is not in the sound reports.

The reports also record that the Companions did not know whether she was a wife or a slave, and said, "If he orders her to veil herself, she will be one of the mothers of the believers; but if he does not order her to veil herself, she will be a slave girl." He veiled her.[5] The ruling was seen by those around him as an announcement of her status.

This does not settle the question of her consent, and the next entries come back to it. It does mean that the story told by those who left Islam has more than the sources give, and a correct account has to start from the sources. Verdict: no report of rape on the day of capture. The question of consent is real, and it is not answered by these reports.

The first thing the Quran does is encourage freeing. It lists "freeing a slave" among the acts that pass the steep path (90:13), and 24:33 tells owners to write a contract of freedom for slaves who seek it, and to give them of God's wealth. The same verse says: "do not compel your slave girls to prostitution, if they desire chastity".[6] The Prophet's act of freeing Ṣafiyya before the marriage followed that line.

Verse 4:24 concerns married women taken in war. Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī reports that after the campaign at Awṭās, the Companions held back from intercourse with captive women whose husbands were polytheists, and 4:24 was revealed, taken as lawful for them once the waiting period ended.[7] The Companions' own hesitation shows that the law was not a licence to take a captive at once.

There is a hard point, and it is not softened here. The classical jurists held that a master has rights over a woman he owns that do not depend on her consent, and this is the heart of the objection by modern readers. Many modern Muslim scholars say that the practice of slavery has ended and the rulings cannot be used. The article on slavery sets out the law and the debate. This is stated from general knowledge and was not checked on a page for this article. Verdict: the Quran pushes toward freedom, restrains the first approach, and does not make consent a condition. That last point is the one a critic is right to press.

Her husband and her father were not killed on the day she was taken. Her father, Ḥuyayy, is placed by the biographers among the men of Banū Naḍīr who incited the confederacy against Medina and who was executed with Banū Qurayẓa. Her husband Kināna is placed at Khaybar. The report in Ibn Isḥāq's biography is that Kināna concealed treasure that the Prophet ﷺ had been promised, that he was tortured to reveal it and was then killed by Muḥammad ibn Maslama in retaliation for his brother. These accounts are from the biography and not from the sound collections. They were read here only in secondary summaries, and the printed page of the translation by Guillaume was not checked.

A fair account must say that these deaths are the hardest part of the story. Muslim writers read them as acts of war after the breach of a treaty, and the writers who criticise the Prophet ﷺ judge them cruel. Both can be argued from the sources, and neither can be dismissed by calling the other one prejudiced. The article on the tribes sets out the Qurayẓa material, and it does not claim the case is simple.

What can be said is that the story of Ṣafiyya does not begin with her marriage. It begins with a war in which her family was on the losing side. A reader who asks how she felt is asking the right question. Verdict: mixed. Her relatives' deaths are in the biography, and they are part of the account.

Later biographical reports, which are not in the sound collections and were not checked for this article, say that the Prophet ﷺ gave her a choice, to return to her people free or to stay and marry him, and that she chose to stay. If that report is accepted, it speaks to the consent question, and the weight of the sound reports does not depend on it.

What the sound collections do show is how he treated her in her household. Anas reports that Ṣafiyya heard that Ḥafṣa had called her "the daughter of a Jew", and she wept. The Prophet ﷺ found her crying, asked what was the matter, and told her: "And you are the daughter of a Prophet, and your uncle is a Prophet, and you are married to a Prophet, so what is she boasting to you about?" Then he said to Ḥafṣa, "Fear Allah."[8]

On the road to Medina he covered her with a cloak, and he sat beside his camel and let her put her feet on his knees to mount.[9] None of this answers the question of consent. It does show a husband who defended a wife of Jewish descent against a taunt in his own house. Verdict: her later treatment is the best-attested part of the account. It does not undo the beginning.

The account does not prove that the Prophet ﷺ was a rapist, because the sound reports do not say so, and they do record the waiting period, the freeing and the marriage. It does not prove that the story is simple, because she was a captive, her kin were killed, and classical law did not require her consent as a slave. A reader who says only the first gives a falsehood. A reader who says only the second leaves a person out of her own story.

Another woman, Rayḥāna, is named in the same arguments. The sources differ on whether she became a wife or remained a slave woman, and no sound report settles it. That is stated from general knowledge, and it was not checked for this article. The claim that she was taken to his bed the night her husband died is not in the sources read here.

An honest critic will want to keep the questions of consent and of war in view, and an honest defender will concede both. Verdict: the sources do not support the charge as it is usually put, and they leave the deeper moral question open. Muslim scholars have long said that the rulings on captives belong to the law of a past age of war, and that the Quran's push toward freeing is the direction it points.

The bottom line

Ṣafiyya was a captive taken at Khaybar. The sound reports say that the Prophet ﷺ freed her, that her freedom was her dowry, that the marriage waited until her period was over, that he consummated it after three days on the road, and that he defended her against a taunt. They do not say that she was taken on the day her husband died or that she was forced. The deaths of her father and husband are recorded in the biography, and they are the hardest part of the story. The law of captive women did not make consent a condition, and the Quran leans toward freeing.

A reader may weigh this differently from a Muslim. What a reader may not do is add details the sources lack, or leave out the details they supply. Allāhu aʿlam.

Notes

  1. Sahih al-Bukhari 371, report of Anas ibn Mālik, read in the English text of the hadith-api edition, where it stands as book 8, hadith 23; the printed page was not checked.
  2. Sahih al-Bukhari 371 and 4200, same edition (4200 is book 64, hadith 240).
  3. Sahih al-Bukhari 2235, report of Anas ibn Mālik, same edition.
  4. Sahih al-Bukhari 5085, report of Anas ibn Mālik, same edition (book 67, hadith 23).
  5. Sahih al-Bukhari 5085, the continuation of the report.
  6. Quran 90:13 and 24:33, Saheeh International translation, read on the Quran.com API.
  7. Sahih Muslim, report of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī on Awṭās, read in English as book 17, hadith 41 in the hadith-api edition; the verse is Quran 4:24, Saheeh International.
  8. Jami al-Tirmidhi 3894, report of Anas ibn Mālik, read in the English text of the hadith-api edition (book 49, hadith 294); its grading was not checked.
  9. Sahih al-Bukhari 2235, the end of the report, same edition: he covered her with a cloak and let her put her feet on his knees to mount the camel.
